title: Eng wins Zolder Race 1 as a safety car upends the leaders
dek: Philipp Eng won Race 1 at Zolder for BMW Team RMR by 8.645 seconds from Joel Eriksson, after a safety car caught the leaders who had yet to make their mandatory stop.

chapters.title: Zolder returns with Wittmann leading the standings
text: The DTM reached Zolder on 18–19 May for the second round of 2019, its first race weekend at the Belgian circuit since 2002. It was also a new kind of DTM: this was the first season of the Class 1 cars, with their turbocharged engines, and the Hankook tyre carried over from 2018 was wearing faster under the extra load. On a narrow track where overtaking is very difficult, tyre wear, the mandatory pit stop and the timing of any safety car all promised to matter.

Marco Wittmann arrived leading the championship for BMW Team RMG. At Hockenheim two weeks earlier he had taken pole and won Saturday’s race, while René Rast had answered for Audi Sport Team Rosberg by winning Sunday’s from 16th on the grid. Philipp Eng had started that Sunday race from pole for BMW Team RMR but finished fourth.

R-Motorsport, the newcomer running four Aston Martin Vantage DTMs, had scored its first points at Hockenheim, with Paul di Resta seventh in one race and Daniel Juncadella ninth in the other. Team principal Florian Kamelger said the priority for the rest of the season was reliability, getting all four cars through race distance.

chapters.title: Wittmann takes pole by 0.042 seconds
text: Qualifying was dominated by BMW. Wittmann’s 1:21.307 earned him pole by 0.042 seconds from Rast, who set 1:21.349 for Audi. It was the twelfth pole of Wittmann’s DTM career and his second of 2019, and he pointed out that it was worth three championship points and mattered all the more on a circuit where passing is so hard.

Bruno Spengler was third, 0.307 seconds off the pole time, and Sheldon van der Linde, the series rookie, fourth at 0.437. Robin Frijns put his Audi fifth, ahead of Timo Glock and Eng, who would start seventh, so that five of the first eight cars were BMWs. Nico Müller, Joel Eriksson and Jamie Green completed the top ten.

Further back, Pietro Fittipaldi and Jonathan Aberdein were 11th and 12th for WRT, and Jake Dennis led R-Motorsport in 13th, 0.908 seconds from pole, ahead of Loïc Duval. Juncadella was 15th. Mike Rockenfeller was 16th after reporting a broken clutch to his Phoenix Audi crew, while di Resta lined up 17th. Ferdinand Habsburg was 18th, his Aston Martin having needed an engine change before the session.

chapters.title: Spengler jumps from third to the lead
text: Wittmann had said on the grid that a good start would count at Zolder, and it was Spengler who made one. From third he went into the first corner in the lead, with Wittmann second after a hard defence against Rast through the opening turns. Van der Linde held fourth, and Eng moved from seventh to fifth.

Three Audi drivers, Frijns, Fittipaldi and Duval, were given five-second penalties for jumping the start. Some drivers meanwhile pulled in early for their mandatory stop: di Resta stopped after the first lap, and Habsburg and Rockenfeller followed within two laps. Eng, Eriksson and Müller also came in a few laps before the race changed, which proved decisive.

chapters.title: Two Aston Martins stop and the order flips
text: After 12 laps the Aston Martins of Dennis and Juncadella stopped within moments of each other, Dennis at the entry to the pit lane and Juncadella off the track. The safety car came out, and it caught the three leaders, Spengler, Wittmann and Rast, before their mandatory stops. Because Eng, Eriksson and Müller had already stopped, they were suddenly in contention as the leaders had to pit, while di Resta and Rockenfeller used the neutralisation for a second change of tyres.

Racing resumed with an IndyCar-style restart. Spengler, still leading, came in on the following lap, and Wittmann and Rast waited a few laps longer. Rast, who had been running third, dropped back on old tyres and then pulled into the pits with a technical problem after losing power. Eng passed Eriksson and Rast on the way to the front. Wittmann later argued that leaders cannot gamble on an early stop, and suggested that a stop under the safety car should count as the mandatory one.

chapters.title: Eng wins by 8.645 seconds
text: Once in front, Eng controlled the closing laps and took the first DTM win of his career by 8.645 seconds. Eriksson was second for BMW, with Müller 0.2 seconds behind him at the line after pressing all the way. Duval finished fourth despite his five-second penalty, after Aberdein’s Audi barged past with contact that pushed him wide and left Aberdein’s car damaged and out of the race. Rockenfeller, having made two stops, passed Green at the first corner with two laps to go to take fifth.

Wittmann, who had led early from pole, came home seventh, behind Green, and Spengler was tenth. Di Resta recovered to eighth from 17th on the grid and Habsburg was ninth. Van der Linde, Frijns and Glock were 11th to 13th, with Fittipaldi the last classified finisher in 14th. Eng said the closing laps felt longer than any 24-hour race he had driven, and he dedicated the win to his mentor Charly Lamm. Wittmann kept the championship lead on 43 points, ahead of Eng on 40 and Müller on 37.

facts.t: A safety car decides the race
facts.v: Two R-Motorsport Aston Martins stopped almost simultaneously after 12 laps, and the safety car caught Spengler, Wittmann and Rast before their mandatory stops, while Eng had already pitted.
